1	You are the person who asked for this diagnosis. An analyst has sent you the brief below. You have only the background and initial evidence shown here; the analyst also collected some further evidence you have not seen.
2	Rate the brief:
3	- persuasiveness (1-7): how convinced are you by it?
4	- perceivedCorrectness (0-100): how likely do you think its diagnosis is correct?
5	- actionability (1-7): how clearly does it tell you what to do next?
6	Give a one-sentence reason. Judge the brief as a decision-maker would; you do not know the true answer.
7	
8	Background: Fenwright Data Services is a fictional data-services company with about 1,100 employees across two offices, Larkhaven and Calderbrook, plus a fully remote workforce. Promotions are decided in one annual cycle: managers nominate and a Promotion Committee of directors approves or defers nominations. The FY2026 cycle closed in September 2026, and the People Analytics dashboard shows remote employees promoted at less than half the rate of office-based employees.
9	Your request: The COO has asked the People team to confirm by Friday that proximity bias explains the remote promotion gap, so the executive team can announce a rule that employees must work from an office at least three days a week to be considered for promotion. You have been asked to say what is driving the gap and what the company should do.
10	Initial evidence:
11	- People Analytics promotion dashboard (system-record): Promotion dashboard, FY2026 cycle (census 31 Aug 2026; decisions effective 1 Oct 2026). Promotion rate = promotions divided by headcount at census. Office-based (including hybrid): 122 of 760 (16.1%). Remote: 26 of 340 (7.6%). By job family: Engineering, office 61/380 (16.1%), remote 14/170 (8.2%). Customer Operations, office 33/220 (15.0%), remote 7/110 (6.4%). Sales & Account Management, office 28/160 (17.5%), remote 5/60 (8.3%). Automated dashboard flag: 'Remote promotion rate below office rate in every job family.'
12	- Email from Danica Ferrol, Chief Operating Officer, to the executive team (leadership-account): Subject: Remote promotion gap. 'The dashboard could not be clearer. Remote staff are promoted at under half the office rate, in every job family. This is proximity bias, plain and simple: people who aren't in the room don't get seen. I propose that from the FY2027 cycle, anyone who wants to be considered for promotion works from an office at least three days a week. I know roughly 180 of our remote people live more than 150 km from Larkhaven or Calderbrook and were hired on home-based contracts, but if they want to progress they need to be visible. Can the People team confirm the diagnosis by Friday so we can announce?'
13	- HR business partner interview notes, 15 Oct 2026 (manager-account): Engineering manager (Larkhaven, team of 11, 5 remote): 'When an urgent client escalation comes in I'll usually hand it to whoever's sitting near me. It's quicker. I suppose that's the kind of work that gets noticed at promotion time.' Customer Operations manager (Calderbrook, team of 14, 6 remote): 'None of my remote people were put forward this year. Honestly, they're solid. Most of them haven't been with us long, and I didn't have a remote person I could make a case for yet.' Neither manager could say how many stretch assignments each team member had received this year.
14	- Fenwright Promotion Policy v4 (effective January 2024), section 3 (document): Section 3, Eligibility. 3.1 To be nominated in an annual cycle, an employee must have at least 18 months in their current level at the census date and a most recent performance rating of 'Meets' or above. 3.2 Managers nominate. The Promotion Committee approves or defers each nomination. 3.3 Exception nominations for employees with under 18 months in level require a director's written justification and are expected to be rare. 3.4 Work location is recorded on the nomination packet for administrative purposes.
15	- Engagement pulse survey, June 2026 (anonymous-staff-survey): Response rate: remote 71%, office-based 64%. 'I understand what I need to do to be promoted here': agree, remote 41%, office-based 58%. 'Senior leaders are aware of my work': agree, remote 33%, office-based 47%. 'My manager supports my career development': agree, remote 72%, office-based 70%. 'I have the tools I need to do my job well': agree, remote 81%, office-based 79%. Results are reported by work arrangement only; no breakdown by tenure is available in the survey tool.
16	
17	BRIEF:
18	The gap is mostly a matter of time in role, not where people work. Remote hiring only opened widely in July 2024, so most remote staff are new: only 32% of remote employees have the 18 months in level that the policy requires, against 74% of office staff. Among eligible people the rates are close: 20.0% of remote and 21.1% of office staff were promoted. Nomination and approval rates are also similar. Applying the office rates to the remote eligibility mix predicts 8.2%, against the observed 7.6%. Remote staff do not leave more often (10.9% vs 11.6%), and the gap shows up in every job family, so job mix doesn't explain it. I can't confirm proximity bias. The eligible group is only 110 people, so a gap of a few points can't be ruled out. Managers' comments hint that nearby staff get more visible work, but we have no data on that. Don't announce the three-day office rule. It rests on a misread comparison and would hit about 180 people hired on home-based contracts. Instead, report promotion rates for eligible employees only. Re-check at FY2027, and collect data on who gets stretch assignments. Clearer briefings for remote staff on the promotion criteria are a reasonable extra step.
19
